defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Fine cracks observed around voids generated by the detachment of α in the cryogenic impact sample; the γ/α interface serves as the crack initiation site for the cryogenic impact sample, contributing to a decrease in crack propagation energy at low temperature. Impact energy reduced about 30 % from 331 J (RT) to 254 J (LNT) due to the 3.0 % α-phase.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: twin boundaries as barriers to dislocation glide (dynamic Hall–Petch effect) reducing dislocation mean free path
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Twin boundaries act as effective barriers to dislocation motion and contribute to the sustained hardening in Stage D; extensive primary and secondary twins provide multi-stage strain hardening at LNT.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: interaction between dislocation and short-range order (SRO)
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: The interaction between dislocation and SRO may lower the critical twinning stress and promote planar slip of dislocations; SRO in the studied steel may reduce the stacking fault energy and critical twinning stress rather than increasing them.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: stacking faults formed at annealed twin boundaries acting as nucleation sites for deformation twins
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: At 3 % LNT strain stacking faults form at annealed twin boundaries; at 10 % pronounced deformation twins nucleate at annealed twin boundaries as a result of these stacking faults.

interfaces.interface_notes: The α phase (~3 vol.%) is uniformly distributed along austenite grain boundaries; the γ/α interface acts as a crack-initiation site under cryogenic impact.
interfaces.phase_evolution: No phase transformation during tensile or impact deformation at either RT or LNT; austenite is highly stable (γ fraction ~97 %, essentially constant across LNT tensile strains per XRD).
interfaces.slip_behavior: At LNT the SFE is higher than the 20–45 mJ·m⁻² range typical for twinning, yet both dislocation slip and twinning occur; slip is planar (SRO/glide-plane softening). Type II grains exhibit single dislocation glide traces, type III grains develop double glide traces, and only a small fraction of type I grains show slip traces.

comparative_performance.note: Designed low-carbon lightweight steel exhibits higher Charpy impact energy than high carbon lightweight steel.
Higher Charpy impact energy than TWIP steel.
Superior specific yield strength; 304 is mechanically unstable (martensitic transformation at low temperature) reducing impact energy.
Ductility nearly 3 times higher than 9Ni steel; also much lower cost due to low-cost elements and simple high-temperature solution heat treatment.
Strength and toughness comparable to Al0.1CoCrFeNi HEA.

service_conditions.stress_state: uniaxial tension and Charpy V-notch impact

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingot with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-6Al-0.1C-0.1Nb-0.1V-1Mo-1W (wt.%) prepared by vacuum induction melting with capacity of 50 Kg under high purity Ar atmosphere.
As-cast ingot homogenized at 1150 °C for 4 h.
Subsequently hot-rolled (HR) into rods with a diameter of 16.5 mm.
HR steel rods solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by oil quenching to obtain equiaxed grain structures with nearly equivalent grain sizes.

L12-type short-range order (SRO) and MC carbide are present.

structures.overall_structure: Impact-deformed structure at both RT and LNT: dislocation substructures characterized by dislocation cells or cell blocks (similar to tensile); no phase transformation in austenite (high phase stability); low temperature promotes formation of deformation twins. Fracture surfaces composed of micrometer/sub-micrometer dimples (ductile fracture) at both temperatures.

unmapped_findings: Measured bulk composition of the solution-treated specimen (wet-chemical analysis, wt.%): Mn 35.14, Al 5.97, C 0.095, Nb 0.11, V 0.10, Mo 1.24, W 0.95, Fe Bal. (Table 1, b0017).

Measured phase compositions (EPMA, wt.%): γ austenite Mn 35.92, Al 5.88, C 0.098, Nb 0.09, V 0.09, Mo 1.12, W 0.86; α ferrite Mn 32.44, Al 6.83, C not reported, Nb 0.09, V 0.18, Mo 1.54, W 1.63 (Table 1, b0017).
Reduction of area: 78 ± 0.5 % at RT and 80 ± 1 % at LNT (Table 2).
True stress values (Table 3): RT 339, 483, 635, 723, 800 MPa at 3, 10, 20, 28, 38 % engineering strain (55 % not measured); LNT 598, 778, 1007, 1148, 1280, 1463 MPa at 3, 10, 20, 28, 38, 55 %.
Corresponding true strains: 3.0, 9.5, 18.2, 24.7, 32.2, 43.8 % at engineering strains 3.0, 10.0, 20.0, 28.0, 38.0, 55.0 % (Table 3).
Geometrically necessary dislocation density ρ^GND (EBSD-α, 10^14 m^-2): RT 0.71, 3.05, 5.64, 7.92, 8.99; LNT 0.97, 2.59, 5.95, 6.93, 9.17, 9.73 (Table 3).

Cell/dislocation-cell block (CBs or DCs) sizes: RT 448 ± 74 nm at 20 % and 282 ± 56 nm at 28 %; LNT 429 ± 76 nm at 20 % and 242 ± 54 nm at 28 % (Table 3); CBs/DCs refined more at LNT than RT at equivalent strain.

Lattice friction stresses: 143 MPa for RT deformation and 389 MPa for LNT deformation; initial grain-boundary strengthening about 108 MPa; twin strengthening contribution 290 MPa at 55 % LNT strain; ferrite dislocation strengthening < 10 MPa (neglected).
Strengthening contributions σ_dis(γ) (MPa): RT 48, 207, 347, 434, 474 at 3–38 %; LNT 58, 240, 379, 469, 504, 646 at 3–55 %. σ_dis(α) (GND): RT 1, 4, 6, 8, 8; LNT 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9 (Table 6).
The process notes flag an inconsistency: the quench is described as 'oil quenching' (b0015) but the tensile specimens are described as cut from 'water quenched steel samples' (b0026).

Taylor factor M distribution along TA: corner values 001 = 2.30, 111 = 3.64, 101 = 3.64; dashed boundary separates M < 2.7 and M > 3.06 regions; 'Twins' regions correspond to high-Taylor-factor orientations (type II and III grains) (Fig. 12).

Schmid factor evolution: RT {111}<110>γ peaks near 3 % strain then declines; RT {111}<112>γ stays higher than {111}<110> throughout; both LNT Schmid factors ({111}<110> and {111}<112>) peak at ~10 % engineering strain (Fig. 4).

Hall–Petch constant K estimated as 0.350 MPa·m^0.5 by linear fitting of yield strengths 267, 258, 251, 245 MPa against D^-0.5 for average grain sizes 8.2, 9.3, 10.8, 12.1 μm at solution temperatures 1000, 1025, 1050, 1075 °C, respectively; K is close to TWIP steels (0.357 and 0.330 MPa·m^0.5).
The grain-type classification (Gutierrez-Urrutia): type I = <001>//TA with ~15° deviation; type III = <111>//TA with ~15° deviation; type II = remaining orientations.
Deformation twinning onset: ~28 % tensile strain at RT vs ~10 % tensile strain at LNT, indicating strong dependence on deformation strain and temperature.
No κ-carbides present in the low-carbon low-density steel (beneficial to toughness); retained ferrite ~3 % refines austenite grains and enhances impact toughness.
XRD austenite volume fractions after LNT tensile deformation: 95.6 % (0 %), 97.3 % (3 %), 95.7 % (10 %), 96.8 % (28 %), 96.1 % (55 %), showing essentially stable austenite with a small BCC fraction.

The intercritical/SFT calculation evaluates γ_SFE (62.64/49.46 mJ·m^-2) exceeding the 20–45 mJ·m^-2 range typical for twinning, so SFE is not the sole decisive factor controlling twinning in this steel.
